# Counting cells and spikes {#sec-count-regression}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(brms)
library(ggdist)
library(patchwork)
library(gt)
library(parsnip)
library(broom)

Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI_f <- factor(cell_data$DPI)
# Centering log-area makes the intercept describe a section of typical size
cell_data$log_area <- log(cell_data$Tissue_Area) - mean(log(cell_data$Tissue_Area))

# Hippocampal neurons in the Sternberg task of Kyzar et al. (2024); the choice of the three
# patients is explained in the text, and the table with all 16 patients is in the same folder
spk <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/WorkingMemory_Hippocampus_Encoding.csv"))
spk <- spk[spk$patient %in% c(9, 11, 18), ]
spk$load_f <- factor(spk$load)
spk$neuron <- factor(paste(spk$patient, spk$unit, sep = "_"))

# Median and 95% credible interval, formatted for inline reporting
summ <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f [%.", digits, "f, %.", digits, "f]"),
          median(x), quantile(x, 0.025), quantile(x, 0.975))
}
```

[The introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) left a promise on the table. It showed you the PDGFR-β counts (@fig-glm_counts_by_dpi), pointed at the floor and the fan, and said that a Gaussian model would fail on them, without letting you watch it happen. This chapter keeps that promise first. Then it goes on to two things the introduction set aside: the fact that every animal's section has a different area (the fix, an *offset*, comes later in this chapter), and the zeros that spike counts, unlike these, are known for. The PDGFR-β counts never drop below about ninety cells, which is a luxury. Spike counts, and most counts you'll collect in an electrophysiology rig, are not so kind.

I'll say something about how the chapter is put together, because it changes scene halfway. We start on the histology counts you know. We fit the Gaussian model the last part would have reached for, watch what it does, and swap the family until the model fits what a count is: first a Poisson, then a negative binomial. Then we read the one number the negative binomial adds, `shape`. Then we give those counts what they've been missing, a denominator. And then we leave the microscope for recordings of single neurons in people, where zeros pile up and we have to decide whether that is a flaw of the family or a feature of the question.

## First attempt: pretend it's Gaussian

Two things about how I'm treating the histology counts for now, so you can hold me to them. First, there is one row per animal (49 animals, 49 rows), so there is no nesting to worry about here. Second, I'm going to ignore something I know. The sections do not all have the same area: `Tissue_Area`, the area of the section over which the cells were counted, runs from about 6 to 20 mm², and it shrinks as the days go by. A raw count therefore mixes "more cells" with "more tissue counted". For now, the count is the count. And because we want the whole time course, including the sham animals at day 0, I'll treat `DPI` as a categorical predictor, exactly as in @sec-linear-regression-multiple, so each day gets its own mean and I don't have to assume a straight line through a curve I already know isn't straight.

I could tell you why a Gaussian is a bad idea for counts, and you'd nod. I'd rather show you, because seeing a model fail on your own data teaches more than being warned about it. So here is the straight linear model, one mean per day and one common `sigma`, fit with the flat `brms` defaults, the same deliberate choice @sec-linear-regression-multiple made, so the data speak with as little interference as possible, and beside its `lm` counterpart.

```{r}
fit_gauss <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit8.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_gauss)
```

The `Intercept` is the day-0 mean (about `r round(fixef(fit_gauss)["Intercept", "Estimate"])` cells) and each `DPI_f` coefficient is how far that day sits from it, just like the categorical predictor in @sec-linear-regression-multiple. Sampling is healthy, and the means themselves are perfectly reasonable summaries. The trouble is `sigma`: a single number, around `r round(summary(fit_gauss)$spec_pars["sigma", "Estimate"], -2)`, meant to describe how far an animal typically sits from its day's mean.

### parsnip

```{r}
parsnip_gauss <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data)

tidy(parsnip_gauss, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

The coefficients aren't wrong. What a model *believes* about the world lives in the data it would simulate, and that's what @sec-mcmc-model-checking taught us to check. So let's ask the model to generate fake animals, day by day, and see whether they look like real counts. I'm using `posterior_predict()` to draw new observations (not just new means) and `ggdist`'s graded intervals to show where the model thinks a new animal would land, with the real animals on top and a dashed line at zero.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_gauss_predictive
#| fig-cap: Where the Gaussian model expects a new animal's count to fall on each day (bands are 50%, 80% and 95% predictive intervals), against the observed animals
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

pp_gauss <- posterior_predict(fit_gauss, ndraws = 1000)

pp_long <- data.frame(
  y = as.vector(pp_gauss),
  DPI_f = rep(cell_data$DPI_f, each = nrow(pp_gauss))
)

ggplot(pp_long, aes(x = DPI_f, y = y)) +
  stat_interval(.width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
  geom_point(data = cell_data, aes(y = Pdgfrb_Pos),
             color = "black", size = 1.6, alpha = 0.7,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Blues", name = "Predictive\ninterval") +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "PDGFR-β+ cells per section") +
  Plot_theme
```

```{r}
neg_share <- tapply(colMeans(pp_gauss < 0), cell_data$DPI_f, mean)
sd_day <- tapply(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos, cell_data$DPI_f, sd)
```

On days 0 and 3 the bands spill below zero: the model thinks there is a `r round(100 * neg_share["0"])`% chance that a new day-0 animal has a *negative* number of cells, and about `r round(100 * neg_share["3"])`% for day 3. Nobody has ever counted minus three hundred pericytes. And notice the second problem, which you've met before: the bands are exactly as wide on day 3 as on day 7, because there is only one `sigma`. The real animals disagree. The standard deviation of the counts runs from about `r round(sd_day["0"], -1)` cells on day 0 to about `r round(sd_day["7"], -1)` on day 7. This is the same complaint @sec-linear-regression-multiple ended on, a single `sigma` that's too generous for the tight groups and too stingy for the loose ones, only now the tight groups are pushed against a wall.

One quieter thing before we move on: the *means* stayed sensible. The Gaussian's failure is in what it thinks is possible around them, in the predictions and the uncertainty, which is exactly where it would hurt you if you reported an interval for a new animal, or trusted the standard errors on the low-count days.

## Same question, new clothes: Poisson with a log link

The smallest change that respects what a count *is* is to swap the family for the Poisson, the distribution for counts of independent events at a steady rate, and the link for the log. That's it: same formula, same predictor, two changes. In `brms` it's one argument. I'm using the `brms` defaults again while we learn the structure; remember the warning from the introduction about priors on the link scale, because later in this chapter I set one deliberately.

```{r}
fit_pois <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  family = poisson(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit9.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_pois)
```

### glm

```{r}
glm_pois <- glm(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, family = poisson(), data = cell_data)

tidy(glm_pois, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

```{r}
b_pois <- fixef(fit_pois)
```

Read these coefficients carefully, because they're not on the scale you're used to. They're on the *link* scale, the log scale. The `Intercept` of about `r round(b_pois["Intercept", "Estimate"], 2)` is $\log(\mu)$ for day 0, so the expected day-0 count is $e^{`r round(b_pois["Intercept", "Estimate"], 2)`} \approx `r round(exp(b_pois["Intercept", "Estimate"]))`$, the same mean the Gaussian gave. The `DPI_f7` coefficient of about `r round(b_pois["DPI_f7", "Estimate"], 2)` isn't "`r round(b_pois["DPI_f7", "Estimate"], 2)` more cells", it's "`r round(b_pois["DPI_f7", "Estimate"], 2)` more on the log scale", and adding on the log scale means multiplying on the count scale: $e^{`r round(b_pois["DPI_f7", "Estimate"], 2)`} \approx `r round(exp(b_pois["DPI_f7", "Estimate"]), 1)`$, so day 7 has about `r round(exp(b_pois["DPI_f7", "Estimate"]))` times as many PDGFR-β+ cells as day 0. This is the price of the doorway: you can't read a coefficient off the summary and add it to a count anymore, you have to translate through the inverse link. What you gain is that the model can never predict fewer than zero cells.

The floor problem is gone. What about the fan? Let's find out whether the Poisson family's *own* idea of how variance should behave matches the data. A Poisson count has one defining property: its variance equals its mean. Here are the two side by side, one point per day, on log axes, with the variance each family says a group should have.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_pois_variance
#| fig-cap: Variance against mean for each day's counts (points), and the variance each family assumes (lines). Both axes are logarithmic.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| warning: false

day_stats <- aggregate(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data,
                       FUN = function(x) c(m = mean(x), v = var(x)))
day_stats <- do.call(data.frame, day_stats)
names(day_stats) <- c("DPI_f", "m", "v")

sigma_gauss <- summary(fit_gauss)$spec_pars["sigma", "Estimate"]
mu_grid <- exp(seq(log(350), log(4000), length.out = 100))

var_lines <- data.frame(
  mu = mu_grid,
  Poisson = mu_grid,
  Gaussian = sigma_gauss^2
)
var_lines <- rbind(
  data.frame(mu = var_lines$mu, v = var_lines$Poisson, family = "Poisson"),
  data.frame(mu = var_lines$mu, v = var_lines$Gaussian, family = "Gaussian")
)

line_labels <- var_lines[var_lines$mu == max(var_lines$mu), ]

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = var_lines, aes(x = mu, y = v, color = family, linetype = family),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = line_labels, aes(x = mu, y = v, label = family, color = family),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v), size = 3, color = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v, label = paste("DPI", DPI_f)),
                  size = 3, min.segment.length = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.3))) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Poisson = "#D55E00", Gaussian = "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "Mean of the day's counts", y = "Variance of the day's counts") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

vm_ratio <- day_stats$v / day_stats$m
```

The Gaussian says the variance should be the same no matter the mean: that's the flat grey line, and the points refuse to lie on it. The Poisson says the variance should equal the mean: the orange diagonal. The points *do* climb with the mean, so the Poisson has the right instinct, but they sit about two orders of magnitude above the line: each day's variance is between `r round(min(vm_ratio))` and `r round(max(vm_ratio))` times its mean, where a Poisson says 1. The day-7 group, for instance, has a variance near `r format(round(day_stats$v[day_stats$DPI_f == "7"], -4), big.mark = ",")` where a Poisson expects about `r format(round(day_stats$m[day_stats$DPI_f == "7"], -2), big.mark = ",")`. The standard summary is the [dispersion statistic]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, the sum of squared Pearson residuals divided by the residual degrees of freedom, which should be near 1 for a well-specified Poisson [@inchausti2023; @gelman2020].

```{r}
dispersion <- function(m) sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m)
disp_pois <- dispersion(glm_pois)
```

Ours is about `r round(disp_pois)`. To see what that means for the predictions, I'll do what we did for the Gaussian: ask the fitted model to generate data and compare. This time I'm using `pp_check()`, and truncating the axis at 6,000 because a few Poisson replicates wander out further than any real animal.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_pois_ppcheck
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive check for the Poisson model. The observed counts (dark line) are far more spread out than any replicate (light lines).
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

pp_check(fit_pois, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000))
```

The replicates (light lines) are lumpy little spikes, one cluster for the low days and one for the high ones, because the model believes each day's counts cluster tightly around their mean. The observed density (dark line) is a single broad plateau. The Poisson family fixed the floor and got the direction of the variance right, and it is still off by a factor of hundreds, which means every interval it reports would be wildly too narrow. A GLM isn't a spell: it gives you a family, and if the family's idea of noise is wrong, the model is wrong, just in a more respectable-looking way.

## Changing one word: the negative binomial

So here is the natural question: can a count model fail and then, with a small change, work? Yes. And the change is the whole point of having a *framework* instead of a menu of separate techniques.

Why is the Poisson too tight? Think about what it assumes. It describes what you'd see if every animal in a group had the same true density of PDGFR-β+ cells and the only randomness was which cells happened to fall inside your counting window. But animals aren't identical. Some mice just have more pericytes in that patch of tissue than others, before you ever count anything. So your count is noisy twice: once because you sampled a window, and again because the *underlying rate* itself differs from animal to animal. The Poisson has room for the first kind of noise and none for the second.

The [negative binomial]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} family adds exactly that second source. It is a Poisson whose rate varies from animal to animal, and it does so with one extra parameter that lets the variance exceed the mean: $\text{Var}(y) = \mu + \mu^2/\phi$, where a larger $\phi$ means less extra scatter, and $\phi \to \infty$ gives the Poisson back [@inchausti2023]. Same linear predictor, same log link. In `brms`, the change is one word.

```{r}
fit_nb <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit10.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_nb)
```

### glm.nb

```{r}
glm_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data)

tidy(glm_nb, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

The coefficient table looks almost the same as the Poisson's: the same log-scale means, the same fourfold jump at day 7. That's the point: the *mean model* didn't change. What changed is `shape` (the $\phi$ above), which the Poisson didn't have, and which is now estimated to be around `r round(summary(fit_nb)$spec_pars["shape", "Estimate"], 1)`: small enough that the extra variance is substantial. Now the same check as before, side by side with the Poisson.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_ppcheck_compare
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive checks for the Poisson (left) and negative binomial (right) models
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| warning: false

p_pois <- pp_check(fit_pois, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000)) +
  labs(title = "Poisson")

p_nb <- pp_check(fit_nb, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000)) +
  labs(title = "Negative binomial")

p_pois + p_nb
```

Now the replicates are broad enough to cover the observed density instead of ignoring it. They aren't perfect: their right tail reaches past 6,000, further than any animal we counted, so the negative binomial is slightly generous with the high counts. That's a much smaller sin than being off by a factor of hundreds. And the mean-variance picture finally has a curve that runs through the points. I'm adding the negative binomial's variance function, $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$, to the same plot as before.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_nb_variance
#| fig-cap: The same variance-against-mean plot, now with the negative binomial's variance function
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| warning: false

shape_nb <- summary(fit_nb)$spec_pars["shape", "Estimate"]

var_lines_nb <- rbind(
  var_lines,
  data.frame(mu = mu_grid, v = mu_grid + mu_grid^2 / shape_nb,
             family = "Negative binomial")
)
line_labels_nb <- var_lines_nb[var_lines_nb$mu == max(var_lines_nb$mu), ]

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = var_lines_nb, aes(x = mu, y = v, color = family, linetype = family),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = line_labels_nb, aes(x = mu, y = v, label = family, color = family),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v), size = 3, color = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v, label = paste("DPI", DPI_f)),
                  size = 3, min.segment.length = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.4))) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Poisson = "#D55E00", Gaussian = "grey40",
                                "Negative binomial" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Mean of the day's counts", y = "Variance of the day's counts") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Strictly speaking, the negative binomial isn't "a Poisson that works": it's a different family. But nothing else in the model moved: the predictor, the log link, the formula, the way we read coefficients. That's what "generalized" buys you. The choice of noise is a dial you turn independently of the rest.

Since the log link now gives us trustworthy uncertainty, let's finally read the effect the way it deserves to be read: as a ratio. Each `DPI_f` coefficient exponentiates to a fold change relative to day 0. A half-eye shows the whole posterior for each ratio, not just an interval, on a log axis so that "twice as many" and "half as many" are the same distance from 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_fold_raw
#| fig-cap: Posterior fold change in PDGFR-$\beta$+ cell count relative to day 0 (negative binomial model, raw counts). The dashed line at 1 means no change.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| warning: false

draws_nb <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb))
day_cols <- c("b_DPI_f3", "b_DPI_f7", "b_DPI_f14", "b_DPI_f30")

fold <- data.frame(
  day = factor(rep(c(3, 7, 14, 30), each = nrow(draws_nb)), levels = c(30, 14, 7, 3)),
  fold_change = exp(unlist(draws_nb[, day_cols]))
)

ggplot(fold, aes(x = fold_change, y = day)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), fill = "#0072B2", point_interval = "median_qi") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)) +
  labs(x = "Fold change in PDGFR-β+ cells vs. day 0 (log scale)",
       y = "Days post-ischemia") +
  Plot_theme
```

Day 3 straddles the dashed line: no detectable change from the day-0 baseline. Then day 7 jumps to roughly four times baseline, day 14 to roughly six times, and day 30 comes back down a little, to about four. That's a delayed surge, which makes biological sense for cells that respond to injury after the acute phase is over, and it's a very different picture from the "no change" a low-count Gaussian's overconfident intervals would have hidden. One caution about the reference point: day 0 is the sham group, so every one of these fold changes compares an ischemic animal at some time point to a sham animal. It cannot separate the effect of the ischemia from the effect of the passage of time, because there are no sham animals at later days (the design limit we met in @sec-linear-regression-multiple).


## What `shape` is really telling us

A few pages ago I reported the `shape` of the negative binomial, said it was "small enough that the extra variance is substantial", and moved on. That was a bit like handing you a thermometer reading without saying which way is hot. So before we add anything, let me go back to that fit and read it properly.

```{r}
shape_draws <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb))$shape
```

Here is the way I like to think about `shape`. Imagine two pericyte-rich animals on the same day after ischemia. Even before you put a section under the microscope, one of them simply has more PDGFR-β+ cells in that territory than the other, for reasons that are biological and not your fault. The negative binomial says each animal has its *own* true density, and that those densities scatter around the day's mean by a multiplicative wobble. `shape` (which I'll write $\phi$, as above) is the dial that controls how big that wobble is: the animal-to-animal coefficient of variation of the true rate is $1/\sqrt{\phi}$ [@inchausti2023]. A large $\phi$ means the animals are almost interchangeable; as $\phi \to \infty$ the wobble vanishes and you're left with the Poisson. A small $\phi$ means animals are individuals.

For our fit, `shape` has a posterior median of `r round(median(shape_draws), 1)`, so before we have counted a single cell, animals of the same day already differ by about `r round(100 / sqrt(median(shape_draws)))`% in their true PDGFR-β+ density. That figure answers a question that comes up at the bench all the time: *if I count more cells per animal, will the noise go away?* The total variance of a count is $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$, so its coefficient of variation, the standard deviation relative to the mean, is

$$
\text{CV}(y) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\mu} + \frac{1}{\phi}}
$$ {#eq-cv-nb}

The first term is the counting noise: it shrinks as the count grows. The second is the animal-to-animal noise: it doesn't depend on the count at all. I'll draw both against each other, with the Poisson (which has only the first term) for contrast, and the observed CV of each day's animals as points. I'm using the CV, not the variance as in the plot above, because the CV is on the scale a scientist thinks in ("the counts wobble by 40% or so"), and it turns the two noise terms into a picture: one keeps falling, the other is a floor.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_cv_floor
#| fig-cap: Coefficient of variation of a count against its mean. The Poisson keeps falling as the count grows; the negative binomial levels off at a floor set by shape (band, 95% credible interval). Points are the observed CV of each day's animals.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| warning: false

mu_grid <- exp(seq(log(300), log(4500), length.out = 80))
phi_sub <- shape_draws[seq(1, length(shape_draws), length.out = 400)]

cv_band <- data.frame(
  mu = mu_grid,
  lo = sapply(mu_grid, function(m) quantile(sqrt(1 / m + 1 / phi_sub), 0.025)),
  mid = sapply(mu_grid, function(m) median(sqrt(1 / m + 1 / phi_sub))),
  hi = sapply(mu_grid, function(m) quantile(sqrt(1 / m + 1 / phi_sub), 0.975)),
  pois = 1 / sqrt(mu_grid)
)

day_cv <- aggregate(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data,
                    FUN = function(x) c(m = mean(x), cv = sd(x) / mean(x)))
day_cv <- do.call(data.frame, day_cv)
names(day_cv) <- c("DPI_f", "m", "cv")

ggplot(cv_band, aes(x = mu)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mid), color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pois), color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = day_cv, aes(x = m, y = cv), size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = day_cv, aes(x = m, y = cv, label = paste("DPI", DPI_f)),
                           size = 3, min.segment.length = 0.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 4700, y = cv_band$mid[80], label = "Negative
binomial",
           color = "#0072B2", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 4700, y = cv_band$pois[80], label = "Poisson",
           color = "#D55E00", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(), breaks = c(300, 1000, 3000),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.3))) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1), labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Mean count", y = "Coefficient of variation") +
  Plot_theme
```

The Poisson (dashed) says that a group averaging four thousand cells should be pinned down to about 1.6%. The observed animals sit ten to thirty times higher. The negative binomial has a floor at $1/\sqrt{\phi}$ (roughly the `r round(100 / sqrt(median(shape_draws)))`% we computed), and the animals sit near it (day 14 a little below, which with a handful of animals per day is unsurprising). This is a fact about the *experiment*, not just about the model: past a point, a bigger ROI or a more patient counter buys almost nothing, because the remaining noise is between animals, and the only cure for that is more animals. If you have ever wondered why your reviewers ask for more mice when you already counted thousands of cells per section, this figure is the reason.

::: callout-tip
### Which `shape` is it? The same number under several names

`shape` in `brms` is the `theta` that `MASS::glm.nb()` prints, and in both the variance is $\mu + \mu^2/\text{shape}$; `glmmTMB`'s `nbinom2` family uses the same form. Other software parametrizes the same distribution with the *reciprocal*, $1/\phi$, so that zero means "Poisson" (a small number, then, is a good sign there, and a large number is a bad one). Whenever you read a paper that reports "the dispersion parameter", check which of the two it is before you decide whether the data are overdispersed.
:::

## "Per what?": the offset

Every scientist has had the following conversation. You report that treated animals have 1,900 PDGFR-β+ cells and the controls have 500. Somebody at the back asks: *per what?* A count is like a receipt with the shop's name torn off: it tells you how many, and it says nothing about how big the window was that you looked through. If sections differ in size, the count mixes two things: how dense the cells are, and how much tissue you counted.

`cell_data` does have that denominator. `Tissue_Area` is the area of the section, in mm², over which the cells were counted. (There's a second column, `Tisue_Area`, with a typo in its name: it is the very same measurement in µm², a million times bigger, so I won't use it; @sec-eda-data-quality shows the check and explains the choice.) I set that aside earlier in the chapter, when I said the count was the count. It isn't.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_area
#| fig-cap: Area of the counted tissue for each animal, by day after ischemia. The area is not constant, and it shrinks as the days go by.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| warning: false

ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = DPI_f, y = Tissue_Area)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = Condition, shape = Condition),
              width = 0.12, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5,
               linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(SHAM = "#D55E00", MCAO = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Counted tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
area_by_day <- tapply(cell_data$Tissue_Area, cell_data$DPI_f, mean)
```

The area falls from about `r round(area_by_day["0"])` mm² in the sham animals to about `r round(area_by_day["30"])` mm² at day 30, which is what you'd expect from tissue that loses volume as the infarct matures. Two consequences. The first is that counts are not comparable across animals as they stand. The second is subtler and I find it more interesting: the area is not noise that's independent of the question, it moves *with* the day, so it will change the answer.

### What an offset does

The idea is old and simple. If the counting window is $A_i$ and the true density of cells is $\theta_i$, then the expected count is the density times the window, $\mu_i = A_i \theta_i$. Take logs, and the window turns into something we can add:

$$
\log(\mu_i) = \log(A_i) + \log(\theta_i) = \log(A_i) + \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots
$$ {#eq-offset}

The term $\log(A_i)$ is called an [offset]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. It is a predictor whose coefficient isn't estimated but fixed to exactly 1, which is how the model says "double the window, double the expected count" [@gelman2020; @inchausti2023; @mcelreath2020]. What remains on the right, $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots$, is now a model for the *density*: cells per mm², not cells per section. The coefficients keep the interpretation they had before (log fold changes), but the thing being multiplied is a rate.

Before fitting I need priors on the log scale, and I'd like to keep them judged on the *outcome* scale, per the warning in [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro). With the offset, the `Intercept` is the log of the density (cells per mm²) of a day-0 animal with a typical section size. Earlier in this chapter the day-0 mean was about `r round(fixef(fit_gauss)["Intercept", "Estimate"])` cells, over sections of about `r round(area_by_day["0"])` mm², so around `r round(fixef(fit_gauss)["Intercept", "Estimate"] / area_by_day["0"])` cells/mm². I'll use `Normal(4, 1.5)`, which puts 95% of its mass between roughly 3 and 1,100 cells/mm², a range that comfortably includes what we saw and is far from "anything goes". For the day coefficients, `Normal(0, 1.5)` allows fold changes from about 1/20 to 20, wider than anything the biology here would deliver (the largest change we saw earlier in this chapter was under tenfold). I keep `brms`'s default for `shape`, an inverse-gamma(0.4, 0.3), which is weakly informative and keeps the parameter away from zero.

```{r}
prior_hist <- c(
  prior(normal(4, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape")
)

fit_offset <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f + offset(log(Tissue_Area)),
  data = cell_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_hist,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_offset)
```

### glm.nb

```{r}
library(broom)

glm_offset <- MASS::glm.nb(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f + offset(log(Tissue_Area)),
                           data = cell_data)

tidy(glm_offset, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

Sampling is healthy. The `Intercept` of `r round(fixef(fit_offset)["Intercept", "Estimate"], 2)` is $\log$(cells per mm²) on day 0, which is about `r round(exp(fixef(fit_offset)["Intercept", "Estimate"]))` cells/mm², close to what I guessed from the raw numbers. And `shape` barely moved: `r round(summary(fit_offset)$spec_pars["shape", "Estimate"], 1)`, the same as before. The offset changed *what* is being modeled, but the animal-to-animal wobble, being a property of the animals, stayed where it was.

What did change is the story about the time course. Here are the fold changes relative to day 0 from the negative binomial model on the raw counts (earlier in the chapter) and from this one (density), side by side.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_fold_offset
#| fig-cap: Fold change relative to day 0 in PDGFR-$\beta$+ cells, as a raw count (the negative binomial model above) and as a density per mm² (offset model). Points are posterior medians; thick and thin bars are 50% and 95% credible intervals.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

day_cols <- c("b_DPI_f3", "b_DPI_f7", "b_DPI_f14", "b_DPI_f30")
d_cnt <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb))[, day_cols]
d_dens <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_offset))[, day_cols]

fold <- rbind(
  data.frame(model = "Count per section", day = rep(day_cols, each = nrow(d_cnt)),
             fold = exp(unlist(d_cnt))),
  data.frame(model = "Density per mm²", day = rep(day_cols, each = nrow(d_dens)),
             fold = exp(unlist(d_dens)))
)
fold$day <- factor(sub("b_DPI_f", "", fold$day), levels = c(30, 14, 7, 3))

ggplot(fold, aes(x = fold, y = day, color = model, shape = model)) +
  stat_pointinterval(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
                     point_size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Count per section" = "#D55E00", "Density per mm²" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)) +
  labs(x = "Fold change vs. day 0 (log scale)", y = "Days post-ischemia") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank())
```

```{r}
fc14_cnt <- exp(d_cnt$b_DPI_f14)
fc14_dens <- exp(d_dens$b_DPI_f14)
```

At day 14, the number of PDGFR-β+ cells per section was about `r round(median(fc14_cnt), 1)` times the day-0 number (`r summ(fc14_cnt, 1)`); their density per mm² was about `r round(median(fc14_dens), 1)` times (`r summ(fc14_dens, 1)`). Both statements are true, and they answer different questions: *there are more cells in the section*, and *the tissue that's left is more crowded with them*. The second is bigger because the tissue shrank while the cells accumulated. If your hypothesis is about the density of pericytes in what remains of the tissue, which is what I'd usually want, then the raw count understates the effect at the later days (at day 7, where the area is close to the day-0 area, the two agree), in the same direction as the atrophy. That's the sense in which the offset is not a technicality: it changed the day-14 estimate by roughly 45%.

::: callout-note
### An offset is an assumption, not a discovery

The offset says the expected count is *exactly proportional* to the area. Nothing in the data forced that: it comes from how the counting was done. The textbook way to check it [@gelman2020; @mcelreath2020; @inchausti2023] is to put $\log(A_i)$ in the model as an ordinary predictor with a free coefficient and see whether 1 is a believable value for it. So let me do that.
:::

```{r}
prior_free <- c(prior_hist, prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "log_area"))

fit_free <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f + log_area,
  data = cell_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_free,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

b_area <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_free))$b_log_area
```

The coefficient of log-area comes out at `r summ(b_area)`. The interval is wide enough to contain 1 (the value the offset imposes) and also 0 (the value that would say area doesn't matter at all). The data cannot tell those apart, and the reason is worth understanding: area and day are tangled up, since the sections get smaller as the days go by, and within a single day the areas are fairly similar. There isn't enough independent variation in area to learn what it does on its own. Comparing the two models by leave-one-out cross-validation says the same thing, that neither is predicting new animals better.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count_loo_area
#| tbl-cap: Leave-one-out comparison of the offset model (coefficient fixed at 1) and the model with a free coefficient for log-area

loo_offset <- loo(fit_offset)
loo_free <- loo(fit_free)
cmp_area <- loo_compare(list("Offset (coefficient = 1)" = loo_offset, "Free coefficient" = loo_free))

cmp_area_tbl <- data.frame(
  Model = rownames(cmp_area),
  `elpd difference` = round(cmp_area[, "elpd_diff"], 1),
  `SE of difference` = round(cmp_area[, "se_diff"], 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)

gt(cmp_area_tbl)
```

That is not a failure of the offset; it's what the exposure in your design is *for*. In an experiment where I know that the count is taken over a window of a certain size, I don't need the data to tell me that the count is proportional to that window. I need them to not contradict me, and here they don't. What I would not do is claim the data *confirmed* the offset. Use it because of the design, check the free coefficient when the data can speak to it (with a lot of variation in exposure at each level of the predictors, this check gets sharp), and say which of those you did.

## A new scene: spikes

Take the histology hat off and put on the electrophysiologist's. The data for the rest of this chapter come from a rare kind of experiment: single neurons recorded, one by one, in the brain of a person. @kyzar2024 released recordings from patients with epilepsy who had depth electrodes implanted to locate their seizures, and who agreed to do a memory task while the electrodes listened. It is a Sternberg task. On each trial the patient sees one, two or three pictures, one after another (the *load*), holds them in mind through a blank pause, and is then shown a probe picture and answers whether it was one of those held. I use the neurons recorded in the hippocampus, a structure every memory researcher has an opinion about. The recordings are open (CC-BY, DANDI archive, dandiset 000469; the study is @kyzar2024, <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-02943-8>), and the script `functions/extract_workingmem_counts.py` streams the files and writes a small table with the spike *counts* I need and none of the spike times themselves. The table has all 190 hippocampal neurons of the release, from 16 patients. For this chapter I keep three of those patients, and I should tell you how I chose them, because it was before looking at any result: the models below are refitted every time the book is built, and a fit on all 24,462 neuron-trials was far slower than a laptop should be asked to be. The patients ran slightly different versions of the protocol (the pictures stayed on screen for about 1, 1.5 or 2.5 seconds), which will matter in a moment, so I took one patient per version, the one with the most hippocampal neurons: patients 18, 11 and 9. The rest of the table is there for anyone who wants to repeat the analysis on everyone.

**One row is one neuron on one trial.** `spikes` is the number of spikes it fired between the appearance of the first picture and the disappearance of the last (the *encoding window*), `window_s` is how many seconds that window lasted, and `load` is the number of pictures shown. The question is a natural one: **do hippocampal neurons fire faster when there is more to remember?**

::: callout-note
### `r format(nrow(spk), big.mark = ",")` rows, but not that many independent pieces of evidence

Each of these rows is a neuron seen on one trial, so they come in bundles: about `r round(nrow(spk) / nlevels(spk$neuron))` trials per neuron, `r nlevels(spk$neuron)` neurons, `r length(unique(spk$patient))` patients. As in the rest of this part, I treat the rows as independent *on purpose* for most of the chapter, to keep it about counts, and I come back to what that costs near the end. The multilevel part of the book is where the bundles become part of the model. <!-- TODO: link @sec-multilevel-glmm once that chapter exists. -->
:::

Let me look at the exposure first, since the whole first half of this chapter was about it. The window is not a constant of nature here: it is a consequence of the design, and of the protocol each patient happened to run.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_spikes_window
#| fig-cap: Length of the encoding window in each trial of each patient, by load. The window grows with the number of pictures, and the seconds per picture differ between patients (about 1 s for most, longer for a few).
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| warning: false

trials_spk <- spk[!duplicated(paste(spk$patient, spk$trial)), ]
trials_spk$per_picture <- cut(trials_spk$window_s / trials_spk$load, breaks = c(0, 1.15, 2, 3),
                              labels = c("about 1 s", "1.2 to 1.5 s", "about 2.5 s"))

set.seed(1)
ggplot(trials_spk, aes(x = factor(load), y = window_s, color = per_picture, shape = per_picture)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, size = 1.4, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"), name = "Seconds per picture") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15), name = "Seconds per picture") +
  labs(x = "Pictures shown (load)", y = "Encoding window (s)") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A neuron firing at a steady rate will emit more spikes in a longer window whatever the patient is remembering, and the longest windows belong to the highest loads. So a raw count of spikes will rise with load even if the firing rate does not move at all. That is the offset problem again, with the twist that here the exposure is tied to the very predictor we are asking about. The table puts the two summaries side by side.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count_spikes_by_load
#| tbl-cap: Spikes per encoding window and spikes per second, by load (means over all neuron-trials)

by_load <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spk, spk$load), function(d) {
  data.frame(Load = d$load[1], `Neuron-trials` = nrow(d),
             `Median window (s)` = round(median(d$window_s), 1),
             `Mean spikes per window` = round(mean(d$spikes), 1),
             `Mean spikes per second` = round(sum(d$spikes) / sum(d$window_s), 2),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))

gt(by_load)
```

The count more than triples from one picture to three and the rate does not budge. If I had analyzed the counts, I would have reported a large, highly significant effect of load on hippocampal firing, and it would have been an effect of the stopwatch. So the model gets the offset from the start.

### The negative binomial, with an offset

The setup is the one we used for the tissue area: $\log(\text{window}_i)$ as the offset, so that the coefficients describe the firing rate in spikes per second. Priors again on the outcome scale. The `Intercept` is the log firing rate of a typical neuron with one picture on screen, and `Normal(0.5, 1.5)` puts 95% of its mass between about 0.08 and 31 spikes per second, which is the span the original paper reports for these neurons (roughly 0.1 to 34). The load coefficients are log rate ratios: `Normal(0, 0.5)` allows rate ratios from about 0.4 to 2.7, a lot more change than I expect from a change in load. The `shape` keeps its default.

```{r}
prior_spk <- c(
  prior(normal(0.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape")
)

fit_nb_spk <- brm(
  spikes ~ load_f + offset(log(window_s)),
  data = spk,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_spk,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit3.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_nb_spk)
```

### glm.nb

```{r}
glm_nb_spk <- MASS::glm.nb(spikes ~ load_f + offset(log(window_s)), data = spk)

tidy(glm_nb_spk, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

```{r}
draws_nb_spk <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb_spk))
```

Look at `shape` first: `r round(median(draws_nb_spk$shape), 2)`. In the histology counts it was about five; here it is below one, and by @eq-cv-nb the neuron-to-neuron wobble of the true rate is about `r round(100 / sqrt(median(draws_nb_spk$shape)))`%, well over a hundred percent. Either these neurons really are wildly different from one another, or the model is using `shape` to absorb something it has no other way to say. The posterior predictive check is the place to ask. For counts, the right check isn't the density overlay of the earlier chapters: with discrete data and a spike at zero, a kernel density smooths away the one thing we care about. A [rootogram]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} is designed for this [@gelman2026]. It compares, for each possible count, how many neuron-trials the model expects with how many we saw, on a square-root scale so that the rare high counts remain visible. In the "hanging" style, the bars hang from the model's expected curve down toward the zero line: a bar that stops short of the line means the model expected more neuron-trials with that count than we saw; one that crosses it means the model expected fewer. I add the simplest zero-specific check next to it, the share of zeros in replicated data against the observed share.

```{r}
zeros <- function(x) mean(x == 0)

ppc_pair <- function(fit) {
  p1 <- pp_check(fit, type = "rootogram", style = "hanging", prob = 0.95, ndraws = 500) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 40)) +
    labs(title = "Rootogram", x = "Spikes in the window")
  p2 <- pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "zeros", ndraws = 500) +
    labs(title = "Share of zeros", x = "Proportion of neuron-trials with 0 spikes")
  p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1.4, 1))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_ppc_nb
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive checks for the negative binomial model of the spike counts. Left, rootogram (bars hang from the expected counts; the horizontal axis is cut at 40 spikes). Right, share of zeros in replicated data (histogram) against the observed share (line).
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| warning: false
#| message: false

ppc_pair(fit_nb_spk)
```

Read the two panels together. The negative binomial gets the zeros right, and if anything overdoes them: the observed share of zeros (the vertical line) sits a little to the left of what the model replicates, and in the rootogram the bar at zero lines up with the expected curve. That is a surprise if you came here expecting a zero-inflation story, and I would rather you be surprised now than later. The model got there by an unusual route, though. With a `shape` of about `r round(median(draws_nb_spk$shape), 1)` it treats every neuron-trial as a draw from a distribution so wide that zeros are common, which is another way of saying that it is describing a very heterogeneous population with one set of parameters. Keep that in mind; we come back to it.

## Is this zero inflation?

In this subset `r round(100 * mean(spk$spikes == 0))`% of the neuron-trials have no spikes at all, and a pile of zeros is the cue for the model that gave this section its name. Here is the picture that helps me. You ask a room of people how many times they checked their phone during your talk. Some of them answer zero because they don't own a phone. Others own one and just happened not to check it. The two zeros mean different things, and no amount of rethinking the distribution of the *phone owners* will explain the first kind: it's a different process, a group of people for whom the count is impossible. A [zero-inflated]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} model writes exactly that as a mixture. With probability $\pi_i$ an observation is a structural zero; with probability $1 - \pi_i$ it comes from the negative binomial, which has its own zeros too:

$$
P(y_i = 0) = \pi_i + (1 - \pi_i)\,\text{NB}(0 \mid \mu_i, \phi), \qquad P(y_i = k) = (1 - \pi_i)\,\text{NB}(k \mid \mu_i, \phi) \text{ for } k \geq 1
$$ {#eq-zinb}

In `brms`, the probability of a structural zero is a second parameter, `zi`, with its own formula and the logit doorway of @sec-logistic-regression. The question I'm asking of the data is the simplest one: is there any structural zero at all? So `zi` gets only an intercept. On the logit scale, `Normal(0, 1.5)` spreads the prior over the whole range of probabilities, which gives the zero part every chance to be large if the data want it. I also set the `shape` prior explicitly to the one used above, because `brms` 2.22's default for the zero-inflated family is a nearly flat gamma(0.01, 0.01), and I want the two models to differ in the structure I'm testing and not in an accidental prior.

```{r}
prior_zi <- c(
  prior_spk,
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi")
)

fit_zinb <- brm(
  bf(spikes ~ load_f + offset(log(window_s)), zi ~ 1),
  data = spk,
  family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_zi,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit4.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_zinb)
```

### glmmTMB

```{r}
library(glmmTMB)

glmm_zinb <- glmmTMB(spikes ~ load_f + offset(log(window_s)),
                     ziformula = ~ 1, family = nbinom2, data = spk)

summary(glmm_zinb)
```
:::

```{r}
draws_zi <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_zinb))
p_struct <- plogis(draws_zi$b_zi_Intercept)
```

The summary answers the question directly. The zero part sits at `r round(median(draws_zi$b_zi_Intercept), 1)` on the logit scale, which is a probability of structural zeros of `r summ(p_struct, 3)`: well under one percent, with an upper limit near `r round(100 * quantile(p_struct, 0.975), 1)`%. The prior would have allowed anything from about 5% to 95%, and the data pulled it to the floor. Nothing else moved: `shape` is still about `r round(median(draws_zi$shape), 2)` and the load coefficients are where they were. So the zero-inflated model finds almost nothing to inflate, and `glmmTMB`, as the frequentist note will show, says so more bluntly.

### A hurdle would not help either

There is a close cousin, the [hurdle]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} model. It also has a "zero part" and a "count part", but it organizes them differently: a first stage decides whether the neuron fires *at all* (crossing the hurdle), and the count of the second stage comes from a distribution that cannot produce zeros. It is the natural model when crossing zero is a distinct event, a cell that either engages or does not. I haven't fitted it, for a reason that follows from the paragraph above: its zero part asks the same question the zero-inflated model just answered, whether the zeros need a process of their own, and what it would add is a different description of that process, not evidence that there is one.

## Where do the zeros come from, then?

If the pile of zeros doesn't need a process of its own, something else has to produce it, and I have a suspect. We have been pooling 190 neurons as if they were one neuron measured 24,462 times. Neurons are not interchangeable. If some of them fire once every ten seconds and others thirty times a second, then a pooled count has plenty of zeros without anything being silent: the slow neurons are simply unlucky most of the time. A zero-inflated model on pooled data would then be mistaking *who is in the sample* for *how a neuron behaves*. The data let us check this directly, because the neuron's identity is in the table. For each neuron, I compute its overall firing rate and the share of its trials with no spikes, and compare the share with what a plain Poisson at that neuron's own rate would give.

```{r}
neuron_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spk, spk$neuron), function(d) {
  rate <- sum(d$spikes) / sum(d$window_s)
  data.frame(neuron = d$neuron[1], rate = rate, n = nrow(d),
             zero_n = sum(d$spikes == 0),
             zero_obs = mean(d$spikes == 0),
             zero_exp = mean(exp(-rate * d$window_s)))
}))
slow <- neuron_tab$rate < 0.5
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_neuron_zeros
#| fig-cap: For each of the 190 neurons, the share of its trials with no spikes against its overall firing rate (points). The curve is what a Poisson at that rate would give for a typical 2.2 s window. No neuron is silent in all its trials, and the zeros pile up exactly where the firing rate is low.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

curve_df <- data.frame(rate = exp(seq(log(0.05), log(40), length.out = 200)))
curve_df$zero <- exp(-curve_df$rate * median(spk$window_s[spk$load == 2]))

ggplot(neuron_tab, aes(x = rate, y = zero_obs)) +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(y = zero), color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Neuron's firing rate (spikes per second, log scale)", y = "Share of its trials with zero spikes") +
  Plot_theme
```

Read the figure from left to right. On the left are the slowest neurons, firing about once every ten seconds, and their trials are empty most of the time, as a Poisson at that rate says they should be. On the right, neurons firing several times a second almost never have an empty trial. In between the points scatter around the curve, mostly above it: a real neuron is not a perfect Poisson process and has quiet stretches, so there are a few more empty trials than a steady rate allows. That excess is real, but it is modest and it is spread across neurons that are otherwise active, which is not what silent neurons would look like. The number that settles it is the largest share of empty trials in any neuron, `r round(100 * max(neuron_tab$zero_obs))`%, and it belongs to one of the slowest: not one neuron of the `r nrow(neuron_tab)` is silent in all its trials. The zeros of the pooled table come, instead, from the slow ones. Neurons firing less than once every two seconds are `r round(100 * mean(slow))`% of the neurons and contribute `r round(100 * sum(neuron_tab$zero_n[slow]) / sum(neuron_tab$zero_n))`% of all the zeros.

The negative binomial we fitted first was doing the same job in disguise. By setting `shape` below one it described a population of neurons with wildly different rates as if it were noise around a single rate, and that is why the rootogram looked acceptable while the story behind it was wrong. The honest fix isn't a zero part, it is to let each neuron have its own rate. In `brms` that is a [random intercept]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} for neuron, `(1 | neuron)`: each neuron gets its own baseline firing rate, and the model estimates how much those baselines vary. I'm showing it here as a preview of the multilevel part of the book, not as part of this chapter's toolkit. I give the standard deviation of the baselines an `Exponential(1)` prior, which on the log scale favors differences between neurons of a few fold over differences of a hundred fold.

```{r}
prior_re <- c(prior_spk, prior(exponential(1), class = "sd"))

fit_nb_re <- brm(
  spikes ~ load_f + offset(log(window_s)) + (1 | neuron),
  data = spk,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_re,
  iter = 14000, warmup = 3000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit5.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

draws_re <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb_re))
```

The model that knows about neurons says that the baseline rate of one neuron differs from the next by a standard deviation of `r round(median(draws_re$sd_neuron__Intercept), 2)` on the log scale, a factor of about `r round(exp(median(draws_re$sd_neuron__Intercept)), 1)`, which is the heterogeneity that the pooled model was squeezing into `shape`. Freed of that job, `shape` rises from `r round(median(draws_nb_spk$shape), 2)` to `r round(median(draws_re$shape), 1)`. By @eq-cv-nb that means that once we know which neuron we are looking at, the wobble between trials left to explain is about `r round(100 / sqrt(median(draws_re$shape)))`% instead of `r round(100 / sqrt(median(draws_nb_spk$shape)))`%. And no zero part was added: the pile of zeros did not need one. A note on the fit itself: random-intercept models mix more slowly, because the global intercept and the neuron baselines trade off against each other, so this one ran with longer chains (`iter = 14000`), and the diagnostics table at the end checks it.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count_loo
#| tbl-cap: Leave-one-out comparison of the three models for the spike counts (higher elpd is better; differences are relative to the best model)

# 4,000 posterior draws per model: the random-intercept fit has 44,000, and the
# pointwise log-likelihood of all of them would not fit in memory
loo_nb <- loo(fit_nb_spk, ndraws = 4000)
loo_zinb <- loo(fit_zinb, ndraws = 4000)
loo_re <- loo(fit_nb_re, ndraws = 4000)
cmp <- loo_compare(list("Negative binomial" = loo_nb, "Zero-inflated NB" = loo_zinb,
                        "NB with a random intercept per neuron" = loo_re))

cmp_tbl <- data.frame(
  Model = rownames(cmp),
  `elpd difference` = round(cmp[, "elpd_diff"]),
  `SE of difference` = round(cmp[, "se_diff"]),
  check.names = FALSE
)

gt(cmp_tbl)
```

The table is a relative statement, but a big one. The neuron-aware model beats the pooled negative binomial by about `r format(abs(cmp_tbl[cmp_tbl$Model == "Negative binomial", "elpd difference"]), big.mark = ",")` elpd units, many times its standard error, while the zero-inflated model is not better than the plain negative binomial (it sits `r abs(cmp_tbl[cmp_tbl$Model == "Zero-inflated NB", "elpd difference"] - cmp_tbl[cmp_tbl$Model == "Negative binomial", "elpd difference"])` units below it, which is what an unneeded parameter looks like: it costs a little and returns nothing). Whatever the zeros are, they are explained by knowing the neuron, not by adding a process for silence. The figure above is the check that says *why*, which is what a comparison cannot do.

## What did holding more pictures do to the firing rate?

Back to the question. I read it first from the negative binomial of the pooled data, the model this chapter built, and then from the model that knows about neurons, because comparing the two is the cost I promised to show you. The coefficients are log rate ratios, so I exponentiate them: each ratio compares the firing rate with two or three pictures against one picture, per second.

```{r}
rr <- function(d, label) {
  data.frame(model = label,
             contrast = rep(c("2 pictures vs 1", "3 pictures vs 1"), each = nrow(d)),
             ratio = c(exp(d$b_load_f2), exp(d$b_load_f3)))
}
rr_all <- rbind(rr(draws_nb_spk, "Pooled (neurons ignored)"), rr(draws_re, "Neuron-aware (random intercept)"))
rr_all$contrast <- factor(rr_all$contrast, levels = c("3 pictures vs 1", "2 pictures vs 1"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-count_rate_ratios
#| fig-cap: Firing-rate ratio (per second) for two and three pictures against one, from the model that pools all neuron-trials and from the model with a random intercept per neuron. Points are posterior medians; thick and thin bars are 50% and 95% credible intervals.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| warning: false

ggplot(rr_all, aes(x = ratio, y = contrast, color = model, shape = model)) +
  stat_pointinterval(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), point_size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Pooled (neurons ignored)" = "#D55E00", "Neuron-aware (random intercept)" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Rate ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.8, 0.9, 1, 1.1, 1.25)) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank())
```

```{r}
rr_re3 <- rr_all$ratio[rr_all$model == "Neuron-aware (random intercept)" & rr_all$contrast == "3 pictures vs 1"]
rr_re2 <- rr_all$ratio[rr_all$model == "Neuron-aware (random intercept)" & rr_all$contrast == "2 pictures vs 1"]
rr_po3 <- rr_all$ratio[rr_all$model == "Pooled (neurons ignored)" & rr_all$contrast == "3 pictures vs 1"]
wid <- function(x) diff(quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975)))
```

Two things to take from the figure. The first is the answer to the question. In the model that knows about neurons, the firing rate with two pictures is `r summ(rr_re2)` times the rate with one, and with three pictures it is `r summ(rr_re3)` times, so per second the neurons fire at about the same rate however many pictures are held, with perhaps a few percent less at the highest load (an interval that just touches 1). The counts tripled and the rate did not, and that is all the offset was for.

The second is the width of the intervals, because I promised to report what treating the rows as independent costs. For *this* predictor the answer is the opposite of what the word pseudoreplication suggests: the pooled interval for three pictures is `r round(wid(rr_po3) / wid(rr_re3), 1)` times as wide as the neuron-aware one. Load changes within every neuron (each neuron sees all three loads), so a model that knows about neurons compares each neuron with itself and drops the differences between neurons, while the pooled model leaves those differences in as noise. For a predictor that differs *between* neurons (hemisphere, patient, brain area) I would expect pooling to be overconfident instead, because the rows would then count as more evidence than they are. The multilevel part of the book is where that gets checked. <!-- TODO: link @sec-multilevel-glmm once that chapter exists. -->

### Does the prior matter?

Here is the sensitivity check for the pooled model, with a narrower and a wider prior on the load coefficients.

```{r}
prior_narrow <- c(
  prior(normal(0.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.2), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape")
)
prior_wide <- c(
  prior(normal(0.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape")
)

fit_nb_narrow <- brm(spikes ~ load_f + offset(log(window_s)), data = spk, family = negbinomial(),
                     prior = prior_narrow, cores = 4, seed = 123,
                     file = "models/count-regression_fit6.rds", file_refit = "never")

fit_nb_wide <- brm(spikes ~ load_f + offset(log(window_s)), data = spk, family = negbinomial(),
                   prior = prior_wide, cores = 4, seed = 123,
                   file = "models/count-regression_fit7.rds", file_refit = "never")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count_sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: Log rate ratios for two and three pictures against one under three prior widths (posterior median and 95% credible interval)

get_row <- function(m, par) fixef(m)[par, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]

sens <- rbind(
  data.frame(Prior = c("Narrow", "Used", "Wide"), Coefficient = "2 pictures vs 1",
             do.call(rbind, lapply(list(fit_nb_narrow, fit_nb_spk, fit_nb_wide), get_row, par = "load_f2"))),
  data.frame(Prior = c("Narrow", "Used", "Wide"), Coefficient = "3 pictures vs 1",
             do.call(rbind, lapply(list(fit_nb_narrow, fit_nb_spk, fit_nb_wide), get_row, par = "load_f3")))
)
sens[, 3:5] <- round(sens[, 3:5], 3)
names(sens) <- c("Prior width", "Coefficient", "Estimate", "Lower 2.5%", "Upper 97.5%")

gt(sens)
```

With `r format(nrow(spk), big.mark = ",")` rows the data swamp any of the three priors, and the table shows it: the estimates agree to the second decimal. The prior is not what deserves our worry in this model. What deserves it is whether the pooled model is the right model, which is what the last two sections were about.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

`MASS::glm.nb()` and `glmmTMB` fit the same models by maximum likelihood, and for the mean parts they land close to `brms`: the offset model gives a day-14 log fold change of `r round(coef(glm_offset)["DPI_f14"], 2)` in `glm.nb` and `r round(fixef(fit_offset)["DPI_f14", "Estimate"], 2)` in `brms`, and for the spike counts the log rate ratio for three pictures is `r round(coef(glm_nb_spk)["load_f3"], 3)` in `glm.nb` against `r round(median(log(rr_all$ratio[rr_all$model == "Pooled (neurons ignored)" & rr_all$contrast == "3 pictures vs 1"])), 3)` in `brms`. The small gap in the fold change is the weakly informative prior pulling a little toward zero. This is the usual story of this book: with a weak prior and a decent sample, the likelihood does the work. The raw-count negative binomial from the start of the chapter says the same: its day-7 log-scale coefficient is `r round(coef(glm_nb)["DPI_f7"], 2)` in `glm.nb` and `r round(fixef(fit_nb)["DPI_f7", "Estimate"], 2)` in `brms`.

Two differences are worth knowing. `shape` is where they drift: `glm.nb` reports `theta` = `r round(glm_offset$theta, 1)` for the histology offset model where `brms` reports a posterior median of `r round(summary(fit_offset)$spec_pars["shape", "Estimate"], 1)`. The posterior of a dispersion parameter with 49 animals is skewed, and a maximum-likelihood point estimate and a posterior summary are two different summaries of a skewed thing, which is also why a frequentist fit of a dispersion parameter from a few animals per group can be unstable.

The second difference is the one the spike data show in real time. `glmmTMB` estimates the zero part at `r round(fixef(glmm_zinb)$zi[1], 1)` on the logit scale, which is a probability of `r format(plogis(fixef(glmm_zinb)$zi[1]), digits = 2)`: the maximum-likelihood estimate has run to the boundary, "no structural zeros at all", and a point at the boundary has no meaningful standard error. `brms` returns a posterior with a median probability of `r round(median(p_struct), 3)` and an upper limit of `r round(quantile(p_struct, 0.975), 3)`, which is a more useful statement: not "exactly zero", but "very small, and here is how small it could plausibly be". With the likelihood flat in a direction like this one, a weakly informative prior on the zero part is doing something practical, not just something philosophical.
:::

## Can we trust the sampling?

This chapter has fitted ten `brms` models, and I said "sampling is healthy" about a few of them. A vague reassurance is cheap. A table isn't, so here are the same three checks as in @sec-mcmc-model-checking for every fit in the chapter: Rhat below 1.01, both effective sample sizes above 400, and no divergent transitions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count_mcmc
#| tbl-cap: MCMC diagnostics for every model fitted in this chapter

source("functions/mcmc_check.R")

count_checks <- mcmc_check(list(
  "Gaussian (histology)" = fit_gauss,
  "Poisson (histology)" = fit_pois,
  "Negative binomial (histology)" = fit_nb,
  "Offset (histology)" = fit_offset,
  "Free log-area coefficient" = fit_free,
  "Negative binomial (spikes)" = fit_nb_spk,
  "Zero-inflated NB (spikes)" = fit_zinb,
  "NB with a random intercept per neuron (spikes)" = fit_nb_re,
  "Negative binomial, narrow prior (spikes)" = fit_nb_narrow,
  "Negative binomial, wide prior (spikes)" = fit_nb_wide
))
stopifnot(all(count_checks$ok))

gt(count_checks) |>
  fmt_number(columns = max_rhat, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(min_ess_bulk, min_ess_tail), decimals = 0)
```

All ten pass: the worst Rhat is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(count_checks$max_rhat))`, the smallest effective sample size is `r round(min(count_checks$min_ess_bulk, count_checks$min_ess_tail))`, and there are `r sum(count_checks$divergences)` divergent transitions in total.

## Where this leaves us

We started with a promise and two loose ends from the introduction to this part, and they turned out to be the same kind of lesson. The promise was to watch a Gaussian fail on counts and to fix it by changing the family, which the Poisson did only halfway and the negative binomial did. The `shape` of a negative binomial is a statement about how different the *units* are from each other before you count anything, and it sets a floor on the noise that counting more cannot lower, which is a statement about your experimental design. An [offset]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} gives a count its denominator: it fixes the coefficient of $\log(	ext{exposure})$ to 1 and turns the model into one for a rate. In the histology data it changed the size of the time course because the tissue shrank while the cells piled up, and in the spike data it was the difference between a count that triples with the number of pictures and a firing rate that hardly moves. It is an assumption of the design, and where the data could not tell us whether it was right, I used it for the reason that we counted over a known window. And when a count has more zeros than a negative binomial seems to explain, zero inflation is the question to ask, and the answer can be no. Here the zero-inflated model found almost no structural zeros, and what looked like silence was neurons with very different firing rates, which a model that knows about neurons absorbs without any zero part.

One shortcut runs through the whole chapter: every animal and every neuron-trial was treated as independent of the others, and the spike data show what that does. For a predictor that changes *within* a neuron, like the number of pictures, ignoring the neurons did not make the interval too narrow, it made it a little too wide, because the differences between neurons became noise. For a predictor that differs *between* neurons (hemisphere, patient, brain area) I would expect the opposite, and the multilevel part of the book is where we check it, with the neuron, the animal and the patient as levels of the model. <!-- TODO: link @sec-multilevel-glmm once that chapter exists. --> Before that, @sec-beta-robust-regression turns to outcomes that are continuous but bounded (the share of an open-field session spent in the center) or heavy-tailed (crossing times), the last two families of this part.
